lead: A vehicle network lets many electronic control units (ECUs) talk over one shared medium instead of one wire per signal. A bus cuts harness weight, cost and connector count. It also makes new functions possible, because one sensor value can reach the engine, brake and dashboard computers at once. This chapter explains nodes, gateways, topologies, bandwidth, latency and determinism, and shows why a protocol must decide who talks when. The same ideas run from a cheap body bus for door switches to a high-speed bus for engine and brake control.
prereq: You need Unit 1 power distribution and harness basics, and Unit 3 sensor and actuator signal conditioning.

sections.h3: Nodes, ECUs and the wiring problem

blocks.text: A node is any device that can send or receive messages on the network. An electronic control unit (ECU) is a small computer that reads sensors and drives actuators; each ECU is a node. A gateway is a node that joins two buses and forwards selected messages between them.

In early cars, each switch, sensor and lamp had its own copper wire back to a fuse box. That bundle is the harness. Adding one feature meant adding wires, connectors and weight. A data bus replaces most of that web with one shared medium, usually a twisted pair. Every node hears the same signal, and a protocol decides who may transmit. A transceiver is the transmit and receive circuit at each node that drives the pair.

blocks.where: L is the number of links for full point-to-point connection; n is the number of nodes. A bus needs one medium and n transceivers, one per node.

blocks.text: With three ECUs, point-to-point needs 3 × 2 / 2 = 3 links; the bus needs one medium and three transceivers. The figure shows engine, brake and door ECUs on one CAN bus, with a gateway to a slower LIN body bus. For n = 12 ECUs, full point-to-point wiring needs 66 links, so 66 twisted pairs and 132 transceiver ends. One bus needs one medium and 12 transceivers. The saving grows quickly with n.

Topology is the arrangement of nodes and links. In a bus topology, all nodes tap the same medium. In a star, each node has its own link to a central hub or switch. In a ring, nodes form a closed loop and each node connects to two neighbours. A vehicle often uses a bus inside a domain and a star-like switched backbone between domains.

The physical medium matters. A twisted pair carries the two signal wires close together, so external noise adds almost equally to both wires. The receiver reads the difference, so common-mode noise cancels. A CAN bus uses 120 Ω termination at each end of the pair. The termination absorbs reflections and keeps the differential signal clean. Missing or extra termination causes ringing and errors, not extra speed.

Fault diagnosis starts at the physical layer: open wire, short to ground, short to battery, or a node holding the bus dominant. A gateway can report which bus is faulty, but it cannot repair a broken wire. The protocol must also detect errors and stop a bad node from blocking everyone.

sections.h3: Bandwidth, latency, determinism and bus classes

blocks.text: Bandwidth is the maximum bit rate, in bit/s. Latency is the delay from a node starting a message to another node receiving it, in ms or µs. Determinism means the worst-case delay is bounded and known, not just small on average. Brake and steering messages need determinism; a door-lock message can tolerate more delay.

Some syllabi group buses into classes. Class A is body and comfort, below 10 kbit/s. Class B is low-speed data, often 10 kbit/s to 125 kbit/s. Class C is high-speed powertrain, often 125 kbit/s to 1 Mbit/s. Class D is safety and time-triggered, with strict timing. These are labels, not fixed law; always check the standard for exact rates.

One medium means shared bandwidth. If two nodes transmit together, their signals collide. The protocol must decide who talks when. CAN uses bit-wise arbitration: a dominant 0 beats a recessive 1, and the lowest identifier wins without losing data. See 6.2 for the frame details. The trade-off is simple: fewer wires, but a shared resource that needs rules.

examples.question: A car has 12 ECUs. Each ECU must exchange one signal with every other ECU. Compare full point-to-point wiring with one shared bus. Find the number of links, transceiver ends, and bus transceivers.
steps: Full point-to-point links: L = n(n − 1) / 2 = 12 × 11 / 2 = 132 / 2 = 66 links.
Each link has two ends, so transceiver ends = 2L = 2 × 66 = 132.
One bus needs one medium and one transceiver per node: 12 transceivers.
examples.answer: Point-to-point wiring needs 66 links and 132 transceiver ends; the bus needs 12 transceivers, a saving of 120 transceiver ends.
examples.check:
n = 12
links = n * (n - 1) // 2
ends = 2 * links
bus_trx = n
saving = ends - bus_trx
print(links)
print(ends)
print(bus_trx)
print(saving)

traps: Counting every pair twice: 12 ECUs need 66 links, not 132. A bus is one shared medium, not a star with a separate link per node.
Confusing bandwidth with latency and determinism: a high bit rate does not by itself guarantee a bounded worst-case delay.
Forgetting termination: a CAN twisted pair needs 120 Ω at each end. Missing termination causes reflections, not more bandwidth.
Swapping bus classes: Class A is low-rate body control, while Class C is high-speed powertrain. Do not treat the letters as order of speed without checking.

quiz.a: A node is any device that sends or receives messages on the network. An ECU is an electronic control unit, a small computer that reads sensors and drives actuators; each ECU is a node.

quiz.q: Why does a shared bus reduce harness weight?
quiz.a: It replaces many point-to-point wires with one medium. Each node needs one transceiver and one tap, so wire count and connector count fall as node count rises.

quiz.q: Eight ECUs need full point-to-point links. How many links are needed?
Why not connect every ECU to every other ECU in a car?
quiz.a: Link count grows as n(n − 1) / 2, so wiring, weight, cost and fault points grow too fast. A bus shares one medium and uses protocol rules instead.

quiz.q: Name bus classes A to D and their typical use.
quiz.a: Class A is body control below 10 kbit/s; Class B is low-speed data; Class C is high-speed powertrain; Class D is safety and time-triggered.

quiz.q: What does determinism mean and why does braking need it?
quiz.a: Determinism means the worst-case delay is bounded and known. Braking cannot wait for an unknown queue delay, so the protocol must guarantee a maximum time.

quiz.q: A gateway joins a CAN bus and a LIN bus. Give one benefit and one cost.
quiz.a: Benefit: slow body devices do not load the fast bus; messages are forwarded only when needed. Cost: the gateway adds delay and software complexity, and it is a single point of failure that must be diagnosed.

beyond: Not for the exam. In production, harness cost and weight push cars toward zonal architectures, where a few domain controllers and an Ethernet backbone replace long CAN runs. Gateways become security and diagnostic borders, so they must filter messages as well as route them.
